stem: What does `git fetch origin` do to your repository?

options.text: Downloads new commits and merges them into your current branch
options.why: That is `git pull`; fetch never merges into a local branch.

options.text: Downloads new objects and updates `origin/*` refs, leaving your branches and files alone
options.why: Fetch only updates remote-tracking refs such as origin/main; your branches and working tree are untouched.

options.text: Uploads your local commits so the remote has the same history as you
options.why: Uploading is `git push`; fetch only reads from the remote.

options.text: Resets your current branch to match the remote one, discarding any local commits you had made
options.why: Nothing is discarded; fetch doesn't move your local branch at all.

explanation: `git fetch` contacts the remote, downloads any objects you don't have, and updates remote-tracking branches like `origin/main`. Your local branches, index and working tree don't change, so it is always safe to run. Integrating the changes is a separate step: merge, rebase or `git pull`.

stem: Your local `refs/remotes/origin/main` updates automatically the moment a teammate pushes to the server.

options.text: True
options.why: It is a local cache, so nothing on the server can change it remotely.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it only changes when you run fetch, pull or push against that remote.

explanation: Remote-tracking branches record where the remote's branches were the last time you talked to it. Git never polls the server, so after a teammate pushes, your `origin/main` stays stale until you run `git fetch` (or `git pull`, which fetches first, or a `git push` that updates it).

stem: Type the command that lists every configured remote together with its fetch and push URLs.
explanation: `git remote` on its own prints only remote names. `-v` (`--verbose`) adds the URL for fetch and push, which can differ if a push URL was set with `git remote set-url --push`.

stem: What is the difference between a lightweight tag and an annotated tag?

options.text: A lightweight tag can move with new commits; an annotated tag stays fixed
options.why: Neither kind moves on its own; both stay where they were created.

options.text: Only lightweight tags can be pushed to a remote such as GitHub
options.why: Both kinds can be pushed; neither is pushed by default.

options.text: An annotated tag is a tag object with tagger, date and message
options.why: Annotated tags are full objects in the database; lightweight tags are just names pointing at a commit.

options.text: An annotated tag can only point at merge commits, not normal ones
options.why: Either kind can point at any commit (or any object).

explanation: A lightweight tag is just a ref under `refs/tags/` holding a commit ID, much like a branch that never moves. `git tag -a` (or `-m`, `-s`) creates an annotated tag object storing the tagger, date and message, and it can be GPG-signed. Annotated tags are recommended for releases, and `git describe` uses only annotated tags by default.

stem: You create a tag with `git tag -a v2.0 -m "v2.0"` and then run a plain `git push`. Does the tag reach the remote?

options.text: No; tags are not pushed unless you push them explicitly
options.why: A plain push only sends branches; use `git push origin v2.0`, `--tags` or `--follow-tags`.

options.text: Yes, because annotated tags are always sent along with every push
options.why: No kind of tag is included in a plain push by default.

options.text: Yes, but only when the tag points at the current branch's tip
options.why: Where the tag points doesn't matter for a plain push.

options.text: No, because tags can't be pushed at all and must be made on the server
options.why: Tags can be pushed like any ref, they just need to be named or requested.

explanation: By default `git push` sends branches only. Push a single tag with `git push origin v2.0`, all tags with `git push --tags`, or annotated tags reachable from the pushed commits with `git push --follow-tags` (which you can make the default with `push.followTags = true`).

stem: Match each command with what it does.

options.text: Registers a new named remote
Changes the URL of an existing remote
Renames a remote and its tracking refs
Deletes a remote and its tracking refs

explanation: `add` creates a remote entry (name, URL and default fetch refspec). `set-url` only edits the URL, which is how you switch from HTTPS to SSH. `rename` also rewrites the fetch refspec and renames the `refs/remotes/<name>/*` refs, and `remove` deletes the configuration and those refs.

stem: What state is your repository in after `git checkout v1.0`, where `v1.0` is a tag?

options.text: On a new branch named `v1.0` created from the tag
options.why: Checking out a tag doesn't create a branch; you need `git switch -c`.

options.text: Detached HEAD: HEAD points straight at the tagged commit
options.why: Tags aren't branches, so HEAD points at the commit itself rather than at a branch.

options.text: Still on your previous branch, with the tag's files overlaid
options.why: The branch is left; HEAD now points at the tagged commit.

options.text: On the remote's default branch, reset to the tag
options.why: No branch is reset; nothing moves except HEAD.

explanation: A tag is a fixed name for a commit, not a branch, so checking it out detaches HEAD. You can look around and build, but new commits there belong to no branch and become unreachable when you switch away. To work from a tag, create a branch: `git switch -c hotfix v1.0`.

stem: Which two statements correctly describe forking compared with cloning? (Choose two.)

options.text: A fork is a server-side copy of a repository under your own account
options.why: Forks live on the hosting service (GitHub, GitLab), not on your machine.

options.text: A clone is a local copy on your machine with `origin` pointing at the source
options.why: `git clone` copies the repository locally and sets up the `origin` remote.

options.text: Forking keeps the copy in sync with the original automatically
options.why: Forks don't sync themselves; you fetch from upstream or use "Sync fork".

options.text: Cloning is a GitHub feature, while forking is a built-in Git command
options.why: It's the other way round: `git clone` is Git; forks are a hosting feature.

options.text: A fork copies the original repository's issues and pull requests too
options.why: Forks copy the Git data only; issues and PRs stay on the original.

explanation: Forking is a hosting feature: it copies the repository into your account so you can push to it without write access to the original, and later open a pull request. Cloning is plain Git and gives you a working copy on your machine. In the usual workflow you fork, clone your fork (that is `origin`), and add the original as `upstream`.

stem:
Alice pushes and sees:

```text
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally.
```

What happened, and what should she do?

options.text: Her credentials expired; she should log in again and repeat the push
options.why: An auth failure gives a different error; this is a history check.

options.text: Someone pushed new commits; she should fetch and integrate, then push
options.why: The remote branch isn't an ancestor of hers, so the push wouldn't be a fast-forward.

options.text: The remote branch is protected, so she must open a pull request instead of pushing
options.why: Protected-branch rejections name the protection rule, not "fetch first".

options.text: Her local branch has no upstream; she needs `git push -u origin main`
options.why: Missing upstream gives "has no upstream branch", not a rejection.

explanation: By default a push must be a fast-forward of the remote branch. Here another developer pushed first, so the remote has commits Alice doesn't. She should `git pull` (or `git fetch` and then merge or rebase onto `origin/main`), resolve any conflicts, and push again. Forcing would delete her teammate's commits.

stem:
Carol's teammate has pushed one new commit to `main`. Carol runs `git fetch` and then `git status`:

```text
On branch main
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 1 commit, and can be fast-forwarded.
```

What has changed in Carol's working tree?

options.text: Nothing: only `origin/main` moved; her branch and files are unchanged
options.why: Fetch updated the remote-tracking ref; integrating the commit is a separate step.

options.text: The new commit's changes are staged but not yet committed
options.why: Fetch never touches the index.

options.text: Her files now match `origin/main`, but the branch pointer hasn't moved
options.why: Fetch never changes the working tree.

options.text: The teammate's changes were merged, and she only needs to push
options.why: No merge happens on fetch; `git pull` or `git merge` would do that.

explanation: `git fetch` updated `origin/main`, so `git status` can now compare and report "behind by 1". Carol's `main`, index and files are exactly as before. `git pull` or `git merge --ff-only` would fast-forward her branch. Before the fetch, the same status would have said "up to date", because it only compares against the cached ref.

stem: On a new local branch `feature`, `git push` fails with `fatal: The current branch feature has no upstream branch.` Which command pushes it and also records the upstream, so a plain `git push` works afterwards?

options.text: `git push origin` with no branch name
options.why: Without an upstream, push.default=simple still has nothing to push to.

options.text: `git push --all` from the feature branch
options.why: That pushes every branch but doesn't record an upstream for any of them.

options.text: `git push -u origin feature`
options.why: `-u` (`--set-upstream`) pushes and records origin/feature as the upstream.

options.text: `git branch --track feature` and then a plain `git push`
options.why: `--track` needs an existing start point; it doesn't create the remote branch.

explanation: With the default `push.default = simple`, Git pushes the current branch only to its configured upstream of the same name. A brand-new branch has none, so Git stops and suggests `git push --set-upstream origin feature` (`-u` for short). Setting `push.autoSetupRemote = true` makes the first push do this automatically.

stem: You cloned your fork (`origin`), and the original project is `https://github.com/acme/app.git`. Put the steps to bring your fork's `main` up to date with the original in order.

options.text: `git remote add upstream https://github.com/acme/app.git`
`git fetch upstream`
`git switch main`
`git merge --ff-only upstream/main`
`git push origin main`

explanation: Add the original repository as a second remote (conventionally `upstream`), fetch it to get `upstream/main`, switch to your `main`, integrate (a fast-forward if you never commit on `main`, otherwise merge or rebase), then push to your fork. GitHub's "Sync fork" button does the server-side equivalent.

stem: Which two statements about pushing tags are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `git push --tags` pushes all local tags, lightweight and annotated
options.why: `--tags` pushes every ref under refs/tags, whatever the tag type.

options.text: `git push --follow-tags` also pushes annotated tags on the pushed commits
options.why: Only annotated tags reachable from the pushed commits are sent; lightweight ones aren't.

options.text: `git push --follow-tags` pushes every tag, including lightweight ones
options.why: Lightweight tags are deliberately skipped by --follow-tags.

options.text: A plain `git push` sends annotated tags but not lightweight ones
options.why: A plain push sends no tags at all by default.

options.text: `git push --tags` pushes tags and also updates every branch
options.why: `--tags` adds tags to what is pushed; it doesn't push all branches.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after creating a lightweight and an annotated tag, a plain push sent neither, `--follow-tags` sent only the annotated one, and `--tags` sent both. Many teams set `push.followTags = true` so release tags travel with the commits they mark.

stem:
`git branch -vv` prints:

```text
* main cb55184 [origin/main: ahead 1, behind 1] add g.txt
```

What does `ahead 1, behind 1` mean?

options.text: One file differs locally and one differs on the server
options.why: The counts are commits, not files.

options.text: One commit is pushed but not yet merged, and one is merged but not yet pushed to origin
options.why: Pushing and merging aren't what the counts measure.

options.text: Your `main` and the last-fetched `origin/main` have each gained one commit
options.why: The branches have diverged: one commit on each side since the merge base.

options.text: The upstream is one commit ahead of the server copy of the branch
options.why: Both counts compare your local branch with origin/main.

explanation: "Ahead N" counts commits on your branch that aren't in its upstream, and "behind M" counts commits in the upstream that aren't on your branch. Both non-zero means the histories have diverged, so pushing would be rejected until you merge or rebase. The numbers are only as fresh as your last fetch.

stem: With a default Git configuration, what does `git pull` do?

options.text: Only downloads remote commits; integrating them needs a separate merge
options.why: That describes `git fetch`.

options.text: Runs `git fetch`, then integrates the upstream branch into your current branch
options.why: Pull is fetch followed by merge (or rebase, if configured).

options.text: Replaces your local branch with the remote one, dropping any local commits you made
options.why: Pull never drops commits; that would be a hard reset.

options.text: Fetches every branch from every remote and merges all of them
options.why: It integrates only the current branch's upstream.

explanation: `git pull` is shorthand for `git fetch` followed by integrating the branch's upstream, by merge unless you choose rebase with `--rebase` or `pull.rebase`. Since Git 2.33.1, when the histories have diverged and you haven't set `pull.rebase` or `pull.ff`, Git asks you to choose instead of silently creating a merge.

stem: A finished branch named `feature` should be deleted from the remote `origin`. Type the push command that deletes it.
explanation: `git push origin --delete feature` (or the older refspec form `git push origin :feature`, which pushes "nothing" to the remote ref) removes the branch on the server. It also deletes your own `origin/feature` ref, while teammates keep a stale copy until they `git fetch --prune`.

stem: A developer clones a private GitHub repository over HTTPS and enters their GitHub account password when prompted. Authentication fails. Why?

options.text: HTTPS remotes only work for public repositories; private ones always require SSH
options.why: HTTPS works for private repositories with a token.

options.text: GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git; use a token or SSH
options.why: Password authentication for Git operations was removed in 2021.

options.text: The password must be URL-encoded and placed inside the remote URL
options.why: Embedding credentials in URLs is insecure and still wouldn't accept a password.

options.text: Private repositories must be forked before they can be cloned
options.why: Cloning a private repository you can access needs no fork.

explanation: GitHub requires token-based authentication for Git over HTTPS: a personal access token (fine-grained or classic) or a credential manager using OAuth. Alternatively use SSH keys. Credential helpers such as Git Credential Manager store the token so you aren't asked every time.
reference: GitHub Docs: About authentication to GitHub

stem: When someone deletes `feature` on the server with `git push origin --delete feature`, every teammate's local `origin/feature` disappears the next time they run a plain `git fetch`.

options.text: True
options.why: A plain fetch never removes stale refs unless fetch.prune is set.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: stale remote-tracking refs stay until `git fetch --prune` (or `fetch.prune = true`).

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after the branch was deleted remotely, a teammate's plain `git fetch` printed nothing and `origin/feature` was still listed. `git fetch --prune` then printed `- [deleted] (none) -> origin/feature`. Setting `fetch.prune = true` makes pruning the default.

stem: You cloned with `--depth 1` and now need the full history for `git bisect`. Type the fetch command that converts the shallow clone into a complete one.
explanation: `git fetch --unshallow` fetches all the missing history and removes the shallow boundary. With `--depth 1` the clone also defaults to `--single-branch`, so to get other branches as well you also need to widen the fetch refspec, for example `git remote set-branches origin '*'`.

stem: In a repository, `v1-light` is a lightweight tag on `HEAD`, and `v1.0` is an annotated tag on `HEAD~1`. What does `git describe` print with no options?

options.text: `v1-light`
options.why: That is what `git describe --tags` prints; plain describe ignores lightweight tags.

options.text: `v1.0-1-g<abbrev-hash>`
options.why: Describe uses annotated tags only: one commit past v1.0, then g plus the short hash.

options.text: `v1.0`, because the nearest tag is always printed by itself
options.why: A bare tag name appears only when HEAD is exactly the tagged commit.

options.text: An error, because two tags are reachable from `HEAD`
options.why: Several reachable tags are fine; describe picks the nearest eligible one.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: plain `git describe` printed `v1.0-1-g66bda67`, while `git describe --tags` printed `v1-light`. Without `--tags`, describe considers annotated tags only. The output is `<tag>-<commits since tag>-g<abbreviated hash>`.

stem: Bob moved the annotated tag `v1.0` to a new commit and force-pushed it. Alice had fetched the old `v1.0` earlier. What happens when Alice runs a plain `git fetch`?

options.text: Her `v1.0` silently moves to the new commit, exactly like a branch would on fetch
options.why: Fetch does not overwrite an existing tag by default.

options.text: Her `v1.0` stays on the old commit; a plain fetch doesn't replace existing tags
options.why: Only `git fetch --tags --force` (or deleting the tag first) picks up the moved tag.

options.text: The fetch fails with an error until she deletes her copy of the tag
options.why: A plain fetch succeeds; it just leaves her tag where it was.

options.text: Git creates a second local tag named `v1.0~1` for the moved version
options.why: There is no automatic renaming; tags have one namespace.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: after Bob force-pushed the tag, Alice's plain `git fetch` printed nothing and her `v1.0` still pointed at the old commit. `git fetch --tags` reported `! [rejected] v1.0 -> v1.0 (would clobber existing tag)`, and only `git fetch --tags --force` updated it. This is why published tags should never move.

stem: Bob runs `git switch -c dev --track origin/main`, commits, and then runs a plain `git push` with the default `push.default = simple`. What happens?

options.text: It pushes `dev` to `origin/main`, because that is the upstream
options.why: `simple` refuses when the upstream name differs from the branch name.

options.text: It creates a new remote branch `dev` and switches the upstream to it
options.why: No branch is created and the upstream isn't changed.

options.text: It fails, because the upstream name `main` doesn't match `dev`
options.why: Git suggests `git push origin HEAD:main` or `git push origin HEAD`.

options.text: It pushes `dev` and every other branch that has an upstream
options.why: That was the old `matching` behaviour, not `simple`.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: the push stopped with "The upstream branch of your current branch does not match the name of your current branch", and suggested `git push origin HEAD:main` or `git push origin HEAD`. `simple` is the safe default: it pushes only when the upstream has the same name.

stem: A fresh clone has `fetch = +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`. What does the leading `+` mean?

options.text: Fetch adds new branches but never deletes any old remote-tracking refs it already has
options.why: Deletion is controlled by pruning, not by `+`.

options.text: Remote-tracking refs may be updated even when it isn't a fast-forward
options.why: If someone force-pushes, `origin/x` is overwritten instead of rejected.

options.text: Tags are fetched together with the matching branches
options.why: Tag fetching is controlled by tag auto-following and `--tags`.

options.text: The mapping applies to all remotes, not only `origin`
options.why: Each refspec belongs to its own remote section.

explanation: In a refspec `<src>:<dst>`, a leading `+` forces the update of `<dst>` even when the new value isn't a descendant of the old one. That is right for remote-tracking refs, which should mirror the remote even after a force-push. Fetch output marks such updates as `+ abc...def main -> origin/main (forced update)`.

stem: A CI job clones with `git clone --depth 1 <url>`, then needs the `release` branch. `git branch -r` shows only `origin/main`. Why?

options.text: The `release` branch is protected and hidden from shallow clones
options.why: Protection affects pushes, not what a clone can fetch.

options.text: Shallow clones can only ever contain one commit from one single branch, by design
options.why: Shallow clones can hold more commits and branches if asked.

options.text: `--depth` implies `--single-branch`, so only the default branch is fetched
options.why: The fetch refspec becomes `+refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main`.

options.text: Remote branches only show up after running `git pull` once
options.why: A fetch would show them if the refspec covered them.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: the shallow clone's refspec was `+refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main`, and only `origin/main` existed. Use `--no-single-branch` with `--depth`, fetch the branch explicitly into a ref, or widen the refspec with `git remote set-branches origin '*'` and fetch again.

stem: On a Linux CI machine with a clean Git 2.5x install (no `pull.rebase` or `pull.ff` configured), `main` and `origin/main` have diverged. What does `git pull` do?

options.text: Creates a merge commit, as it always has
options.why: Since 2.33.1 Git won't pick merge or rebase for you when histories diverge.

options.text: Rebases the local commits on top of `origin/main` automatically, as the default
options.why: Rebase is never the implicit default.

options.text: Stops with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches"
options.why: You must choose: `--rebase`, `--no-rebase` or `--ff-only`, or set it in config.

options.text: Discards the local commits and fast-forwards to `origin/main`
options.why: Pull never discards commits.

explanation: Git 2.27 began warning, and from 2.33.1 a pull of diverged histories with no `pull.rebase`/`pull.ff` setting fails and lists the options. Git for Windows ships a system `gitconfig` with `pull.rebase = false`, so on Windows the same pull quietly merges; verified with `git config --show-origin`.

stem: A team wants `git pull` never to create a merge commit on their machines. Which two settings achieve that? (Choose two.)

options.text: `pull.ff = only`
options.why: Pull then refuses unless it can fast-forward, so no merge commit is made.

options.text: `pull.rebase = true`
options.why: Local commits are replayed on the upstream instead of being merged.

options.text: `push.autoSetupRemote = true`
options.why: That only sets the upstream on first push.

options.text: `fetch.prune = true`
options.why: That removes stale remote-tracking refs; it doesn't affect integration.

options.text: `merge.ff = true`
options.why: That is the default and still allows merge commits when needed.

explanation: `pull.ff = only` makes pull fail when a fast-forward isn't possible; verified with Git 2.55, where `-c pull.ff=only pull` refused rather than merging. `pull.rebase = true` rebases local commits on top of the fetched upstream. Either way, no merge commit comes from pulling.

stem: Alice pushes `feature` with an upstream, then runs `git push origin --delete feature`. What does `git branch -vv` show next to her local `feature`?

options.text: `[origin/feature]`, unchanged until she runs `git fetch --prune`
options.why: Her own push already removed her origin/feature ref.

options.text: `[origin/feature: gone]`
options.why: Her upstream setting remains, but the ref it points at no longer exists.

options.text: Nothing, because deleting the remote branch also deleted her local one
options.why: Deleting the remote branch never touches local branches.

options.text: `[origin/main]`, because Git switches the upstream to the default branch
options.why: Git doesn't reassign upstreams.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: `git push --delete` also removes the pusher's own remote-tracking ref, so `branch -vv` showed `[origin/feature: gone]`. The `branch.feature.remote/merge` config remains, which is why a later `git pull` complains that no such ref was fetched. Other clones keep a stale `origin/feature` until they prune.

stem: Match each push command with what it does on the remote `origin`.

options.text: Updates remote `main` with your current commit, whatever your branch is called
Deletes the remote branch `old`
Updates remote `release` from your local `feature`
Sends a single ref, here the tag `v1.0`

explanation: A push refspec is `<local>:<remote>`. An empty source (`:old`) deletes the destination, `HEAD:main` pushes whatever is checked out to `main`, and naming one ref, such as a tag, pushes just that ref to the same name.

stem: How does a partial clone with `--filter=blob:none` differ from a shallow clone with `--depth 1`?

options.text: It downloads every blob but drops old commits from the history
options.why: That is closer to shallow; blob:none keeps commits and skips blobs.

options.text: It has the full commit history but fetches file contents on demand
options.why: `git log` works fully; old file versions download when first needed.

options.text: It clones only one directory, so other paths can never be checked out
options.why: That describes sparse checkout, not a blob filter.

options.text: It is the same as a shallow clone, just spelled differently
options.why: They trade off differently: history vs file contents.

explanation: A blobless partial clone fetches all commits and trees but only the blobs needed for the checkout. Older blobs are fetched lazily from the promisor remote when you diff or check out old versions. A shallow clone truncates history instead, which breaks `log`, `blame` and merge-base calculations beyond the boundary.
reference: GitHub Blog: Get up to speed with partial clone and shallow clone

stem: A contributor opens a pull request from their fork. The repository's GitHub Actions workflow runs on `pull_request` and needs `DEPLOY_KEY`, a repository secret. What happens?

options.text: The run gets no repository secrets and only a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`
options.why: Secrets are withheld from fork PRs so contributed code can't steal them.

options.text: The run gets the secret, because the workflow file comes from the base repository
options.why: For `pull_request`, the workflow comes from the PR's merge commit, so secrets are withheld.

options.text: The run is blocked until the contributor adds the secret to their fork
options.why: Their fork's secrets aren't used for the upstream run either.

options.text: The workflow fails to start because forks can't trigger workflows
options.why: Fork PRs can trigger workflows; first-time contributors may need approval.

explanation: For workflows triggered by `pull_request` from a fork, GitHub passes no repository secrets (other than `GITHUB_TOKEN`) and gives `GITHUB_TOKEN` read-only permissions. Steps that need secrets must run on trusted events, or very carefully under `pull_request_target`, which runs the base branch's workflow with secrets and must never check out and run the untrusted PR code.
reference: GitHub Docs: Using secrets in GitHub Actions

stem: A colleague pushed a new branch `hotfix`. You run `git fetch`, then `git switch hotfix`, with no local branch of that name. What happens?

options.text: It fails, because `hotfix` is not a local branch
options.why: Switch's "guess" mode handles exactly this case.

options.text: Git creates local `hotfix` from `origin/hotfix` and sets it as upstream
options.why: With exactly one matching remote-tracking branch, Git creates and tracks it.

options.text: HEAD detaches at `origin/hotfix`
options.why: Detaching needs `--detach` or switching to the remote ref by full name.

options.text: Git creates `hotfix` from your current commit, with no upstream configured at all
options.why: The new branch starts from origin/hotfix, not from HEAD.

explanation: `git switch <name>` (and `checkout`) has `--guess` on by default: if no local branch exists and exactly one remote has a matching branch, Git runs the equivalent of `git switch -c hotfix --track origin/hotfix`. If two remotes both have `hotfix`, it refuses unless `checkout.defaultRemote` picks one.

stem: Type the configuration key that, when set to `true`, makes the first `git push` of a new branch automatically create the remote branch and set it as the upstream.
explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: `git -c push.autoSetupRemote=true push` on a new branch printed `* [new branch] feature -> feature` and `branch 'feature' set up to track 'origin/feature'`. It saves typing `-u origin <branch>`.

stem: Put the steps of `git pull --rebase` on a branch with two local commits in the order Git performs them.

options.text: Fetch from the remote and update `origin/main`
Find the local commits that are not in the upstream
Move the branch to the new upstream commit
Replay the local commits one by one on top of it

explanation: `pull --rebase` fetches first, then rebases: it works out which local commits aren't upstream, resets the branch to the fetched upstream, and re-applies those commits, which get new IDs. The result is linear history without a merge commit. If a replayed commit conflicts, you resolve it and `git rebase --continue`.

stem: Alice is on `feature`, which has an upstream of `origin/feature`. A teammate deleted that branch on the server, and Alice ran `git fetch --prune`. What does `git pull` print?

options.text: `Already up to date.`
options.why: There is nothing to compare against; pull can't find the configured ref.

options.text: That the ref `refs/heads/feature` is configured to merge but was not fetched
options.why: The upstream config remains, but the remote branch no longer exists.

options.text: That it merged `origin/main` instead, the default branch
options.why: Pull never falls back to another branch.

options.text: A rejection saying the branch is not a fast-forward of the remote feature branch
options.why: Nothing is pushed or merged, so there is no fast-forward check.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: pull printed "Your configuration specifies to merge with the ref 'refs/heads/feature' from the remote, but no such ref was fetched." The fix is to set a new upstream (`git branch --set-upstream-to origin/main`) or `git branch --unset-upstream` and delete the finished branch.

stem: Which three statements about tags and fetching are true for Git 2.5x? (Choose three.)

options.text: A plain fetch auto-follows tags that point into the history it downloads
options.why: Tags pointing at fetched commits come along unless `--no-tags` is set.

options.text: A plain fetch never moves a tag you already have, even if it moved upstream
options.why: Verified: the old tag stayed after the upstream was force-updated.

options.text: `git fetch --tags --force` updates local tags that moved upstream
options.why: Without --force, --tags reports "would clobber existing tag" instead.

options.text: Tags are namespaced per remote, like `origin/v1.0`
options.why: All tags share the single refs/tags namespace.

options.text: `git fetch --prune` deletes local tags that the remote no longer has
options.why: Tags are pruned only with `--prune-tags`.

explanation: Tags live in one global namespace (`refs/tags/*`), so Git is conservative: auto-following brings in new tags, but existing tags aren't overwritten unless you pass `--force`. `--prune` removes stale remote-tracking branches only; tags need `--prune-tags`.

stem: A shallow single-branch clone has `fetch = +refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main`. You run `git fetch origin topic`. Where does `topic` end up?

options.text: In `refs/remotes/origin/topic`, created automatically
options.why: The configured refspec doesn't cover topic, so no remote-tracking ref is created.

options.text: Only in `FETCH_HEAD`; `git branch -r` still lists only `origin/main`
options.why: Command-line fetches update remote-tracking refs only when the configured refspec matches.

options.text: In a new local branch named `topic`, checked out automatically
options.why: Fetch never creates or checks out local branches.

options.text: Nowhere: the fetch fails because the clone was made as a single-branch clone
options.why: Fetching an explicit ref works even in a single-branch clone.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: the fetch printed `* branch topic -> FETCH_HEAD`, and `git branch -r` still showed only `origin/main`. Git updates remote-tracking refs opportunistically only when a configured refspec maps the ref. Use `git fetch origin topic:refs/remotes/origin/topic` or widen the refspec with `git remote set-branches --add origin topic`.

stem: In a fork workflow, `main` tracks `upstream/main` (the original project), `origin` is your fork, and you set `git config remote.pushDefault origin`. Where do `git pull` and a plain `git push` go?

options.text: Both go to `upstream`, because that is the branch's upstream
options.why: remote.pushDefault overrides where pushes go.

options.text: `git pull` reads from `upstream`; `git push` writes `main` to `origin`
options.why: This is the triangular workflow: pull from the source, push to your fork.

options.text: Both go to `origin`, because pushDefault changes the upstream too
options.why: pushDefault affects pushes only; pull still uses branch.main.remote.

options.text: `git push` fails, because the upstream remote differs from the push remote
options.why: With a different push remote, push.default=simple behaves like current.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: with `main` tracking `upstream/main` and `remote.pushDefault = origin`, `git push` created `main` on the fork (`To ../fork.git * [new branch] main -> main`), while `git status` still compared against `upstream/main`. When the push remote differs from the pull remote, `simple` pushes to a branch of the same name.

stem: A developer's `git pull` on diverged branches quietly creates a merge commit on Windows, but the same command fails on the Linux CI image with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches". Neither machine has user-level `pull.*` settings. What explains the difference?

options.text: Windows Git is older and predates the divergent-branches check
options.why: Recent Git for Windows has the check; something configures it away.

options.text: Git for Windows' system `gitconfig` sets `pull.rebase = false`
options.why: With a pull mode configured, Git doesn't ask; `git config --show-origin` reveals it.

options.text: Line-ending conversion makes Windows see the histories as compatible
options.why: `core.autocrlf` doesn't affect how histories are integrated.

options.text: The CI image runs a detached HEAD, so pull can't merge
options.why: A detached HEAD gives a different error ("You are not currently on a branch").

explanation: Verified on this machine: `git config --show-origin --get-all pull.rebase` printed `file:C:/Program Files/Git/etc/gitconfig false`. Because a choice is configured at system level, pull merges without prompting. On a clean Linux install nothing is set, so Git 2.33.1+ stops and asks. Teams should set `pull.rebase` or `pull.ff` explicitly in shared setup.

stem: A contributor opens a pull request from their fork to `acme/app`. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: With "Allow edits by maintainers", maintainers can push to the PR's head branch
options.why: GitHub grants maintainers write access to that branch in the fork.

options.text: The PR's commits are readable on the upstream via a `refs/pull/<n>/head` ref
options.why: GitHub stores the PR head under refs/pull/<n>/head in the base repository.

options.text: Opening the PR gives the contributor write access to `acme/app`
options.why: Contributors need no write access, and opening a PR doesn't grant it.

options.text: Maintainers can push to every branch of the contributor's fork
options.why: The permission covers only the PR's head branch.

options.text: The fork must be private so its branches stay hidden from others
options.why: Forks of public repositories are public.

explanation: GitHub exposes every pull request on the base repository as `refs/pull/<number>/head` (and `/merge`), so maintainers can `git fetch origin pull/123/head:pr-123` without adding the fork as a remote. The "Allow edits by maintainers" checkbox lets people with push access to the base repo push to the PR's head branch only.
reference: GitHub Docs: Allowing changes to a pull request branch created from a fork

stem: Your company deletes a private repository. A contractor had forked it to their personal account while they had access. What happens to the fork, per GitHub's documented behaviour?

options.text: Forks of a private repository are deleted when it is deleted
options.why: Private forks depend on the upstream repository and are removed with it.

options.text: The fork becomes the new root of the network and stays private
options.why: That is what happens with public repositories.

options.text: The fork turns public automatically so its history is preserved
options.why: Visibility never changes automatically like this.

options.text: The fork is kept but becomes read-only until the owner transfers it
options.why: There is no read-only state for orphaned private forks.

explanation: GitHub documents that deleting a private repository deletes all of its forks, and that losing access to a private repository removes your fork of it. Deleting a public repository instead promotes one fork to be the new network root. Neither protects data already cloned to someone's machine, so secrets must still be rotated.
reference: GitHub Docs: What happens to forks when a repository is deleted or changes visibility

stem: Put the steps for renaming a repository's default branch from `master` to `main` (with teammates) in a safe order.

options.text: `git branch -m master main` locally
`git push -u origin main`
Set `main` as the default branch in the hosting service's settings
Update branch protection and CI references, then delete `master` on the remote
Teammates run `git fetch`, `git branch -m master main` and `git branch -u origin/main`

explanation: Create `main` on the remote before switching the default. GitHub's own rename feature retargets PRs and redirects the old name. Delete the old branch only after the default, protections and pipelines no longer point at it. Each clone then renames its local branch and resets its upstream.

stem: After `git fetch`, you see `[origin/feature: ahead 3, behind 2]`, but you made no new commits since your last push, which succeeded. What most likely happened?

options.text: Your three commits were never really uploaded by the push
options.why: A successful push updates origin/feature to your commits, so they were on the server.

options.text: Someone rewrote and force-pushed `feature`, replacing your commits
options.why: Your old commits are no longer in the rewritten branch, which also has 2 new ones.

options.text: A teammate merged `feature` into `main` on the server
options.why: That changes main, not the commits counted for feature.

options.text: Your remote-tracking ref is stale; fetching again will show "up to date"
options.why: You just fetched; the counts already reflect the server.

explanation: Being "ahead" with no new local commits means commits you had (and pushed) are missing from the server's branch now, the signature of a rebase plus force-push. Fetch output shows `+ old...new feature -> origin/feature (forced update)`. Coordinate before resetting or rebasing onto the new history, so nobody's work is lost.

stem: `git fetch --prune` also deletes local tags that no longer exist on the remote.

options.text: True
options.why: Only `--prune-tags` (or `fetch.pruneTags`) prunes tags.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `--prune` removes stale remote-tracking branches only; tags need `--prune-tags`.

explanation: Tags are local refs in one shared namespace, not remote-tracking refs, so normal pruning leaves them alone. `git fetch --prune --prune-tags` (or `fetch.pruneTags = true`) makes local tags mirror the remote, deleting local tags that the remote doesn't have, including ones you created and never pushed.

stem: Which three statements about remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main` are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: They are updated by fetch and pull, and by your own successful pushes
options.why: A push also moves the matching origin/* ref on your machine.

options.text: You can't commit to them directly; switching to one detaches HEAD
options.why: They mirror the remote and aren't meant to be moved by local commits.

options.text: `git status` ahead/behind counts are only as current as your last fetch
options.why: Status compares against the cached ref without contacting the server.

options.text: They live under `.git/refs/heads/` alongside local branches
options.why: They live under refs/remotes/<remote>/.

options.text: The server updates them on your machine whenever its branches change
options.why: Nothing updates them without a fetch, pull or push.

explanation: Remote-tracking branches (`refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>`) are your local record of the remote's branches. Only fetching, pulling or pushing changes them. Because `git status` uses them without network access, run `git fetch` before trusting "up to date".

stem: Alice's push was rejected with `(fetch first)`, yet `git status -sb` immediately afterwards showed `## main...origin/main [ahead 1]`, not "diverged". Why?

options.text: The rejected push rolled back the teammate's commit on the server
options.why: A rejected push changes nothing on the server.

options.text: Her `origin/main` is stale: the rejected push doesn't fetch the new commit
options.why: Status compares with the last-fetched ref; after `git fetch` it reports diverged.

options.text: `-sb` hides "behind" counts, so only "ahead" is shown
options.why: The short format shows both ahead and behind when both apply.

options.text: The teammate's commit was on another branch that only looked like `main` here
options.why: The rejection itself proves remote main has commits she lacks.

explanation: Verified with Git 2.55: right after the rejection, `git status -sb` reported `[ahead 1]`. After `git fetch`, `git branch -vv` showed `[origin/main: ahead 1, behind 1]` and status said the branches had diverged. A rejected push tells you the server moved, but only a fetch updates your local view of it.
